Summary
Hyperacute rejection (HAR) in xenotransplantation typically destroys vascularized porcine grafts within minutes to hours after reperfusion because preformed xenoreactive natural antibodies bind endothelial carbohydrate antigens (notably α-Gal), activate complement, and trigger endothelial injury, thrombosis, and early cellular infiltration; in contrast, acellular or genetically engineered grafts can evade HAR and achieve much longer survival, but later barriers (e.g., thrombotic microangiopathy, NK/macrophage cytotoxicity, and variable infectious/immune risks) cause outcomes to differ widely across studies and species. <cite id="51f1e6f5-2">In pig–primate settings, HAR is classically a humoral response with deposition of xenoreactive natural antibodies and complement activation in vascularized organs within a time window of minutes to hours</cite> and <cite id="58c0d31b-1">is mediated by pre-existing natural antibodies against the galactose-α1,3-galactose (α-Gal) antigen with activation of a complement cascade</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-0">Genetically engineered pigs that eliminate α-Gal (GGTA1 knockout) and/or express human complement regulators (CD46/CD55/CD59) markedly reduce or abolish HAR and have produced years-long survival in baboons and nonhuman primates</cite>.

When xenotransplantation fails due to hyperacute rejection
- Immediate window and vascularized grafts: <cite id="58c0d31b-1">HAR begins as soon as donor xenoantigens contact recipient antibodies and complement, and in pig-to-primate heart or kidney allografts, full complement activation and endothelial injury occur within minutes to hours, rapidly destroying function and leading to graft loss</cite>. <cite id="51f1e6f5-2">Pathologically, early vascular thrombosis, red-cell extravasation, and endothelial activation dominate, with acute cellular infiltrates adding to dysfunction</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-4">Earlier preclinical models without complement-regulatory transgenes typically showed intravascular thrombosis and ischemic injury within hours, consistent with HAR</cite>.
- Antibody sources and ABO context: <cite id="58c0d31b-1">Human xenoreactive natural IgM antibodies recognize α-Gal, absent in old world monkeys and humans due to loss of GGTA1, explaining why primates and humans mount strong anti-α-Gal responses to pig grafts</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-3">ABO incompatibility in allografts is often less susceptible to hyperacute rejection because erythrocyte antigens differ from endothelial core structures and many ABO-incompatible grafts tolerate via complement-regulatory mechanisms, although porcine complement regulators may be less effective against heterologous human complement</cite>. <cite id="51f1e6f5-0">Historically, survival could be prolonged when plasma xenoantigen drivers were removed or antibodies inhibited, underscoring the central role of recipient antibodies and donor antigens in HAR</cite>.
- Endothelial antigens beyond α-Gal: <cite id="58c0d31b-0">Pigs also express Neu5Gc and Sda blood group antigens that bind human antibodies; double/triple knockouts of α-Gal, Neu5Gc, and Sda reduce antibody binding in vitro</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-4">Even with α-Gal knockout, residual thrombotic complications and immune recognition persist, requiring additional genetic and immunologic interventions</cite>.

Why engineered pigs and modern protocols change failure timelines
- Removing the primary antigen and complement “landmine”: <cite id="58c0d31b-2">Porcine GGTA1 knockout markedly increases survival of xenografts in baboons (up to months) by greatly reducing hyperacute rejection</cite>, and <cite id="58c0d31b-0">in heart and kidney models, α-Gal–deficient grafts have survived 499 days in rhesus macaques and up to ~3 years in baboons when combined with human complement regulators</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-1">Adding human complement regulatory genes (CD55, CD46, CD59) suppresses complement activation at the graft surface and reduces HAR frequency to near disappearance</cite>.
- Beyond HAR: later immune axes and coagulation become dominant. <cite id="58c0d31b-4">The porcine coagulation system is incompatible with primates, leading to fibrin deposition and thrombosis even when HAR is mitigated</cite>, and <cite id="58c0d31b-2">coagulation dysregulation contributes to thrombotic microangiopathy in the graft and consumptive coagulopathy in the recipient</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-0">Transgenic strategies also address NK and T-cell cytotoxicity (e.g., HLA-E coexpression with hCD46) to reduce endothelial activation and complement deposition</cite>.
- Human-first proof-of-concept with mixed pathology: <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">The January 2022 first-in-human genetically edited pig heart showed 60 days survival with histology lacking microvascular thrombosis, highlighting atypical xenograft pathology and underscoring that HAR mechanisms in humans remain incompletely understood</cite>.

Why survival outcomes conflict across reports
- Species, organ, and genetic engineering vary: <cite id="51f1e6f5-4">HAR can destroy vascularized organs in a few minutes to hours, but outcomes improve with donor antigen reduction and complement inhibition, yielding multi-year survival in genetically engineered pigs in primates</cite>, whereas <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">earlier human whole-organ attempts failed within days and showed unexpected pathology</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-0">Early nonengineered porcine hearts failed within days to weeks, while α-Gal KO plus hCD46/CD55 lines extended survival to hundreds of days in baboons and even multi-years in primates</cite>.
- Graft type dictates immune exposure and kinetics. <cite id="58c0d31b-4">Whole organs expose large endothelial surfaces with α-Gal and prothrombotic signals, promoting rapid complement activation and thrombosis</cite>, but <cite id="5aa20e76-0">decellularized acellular matrices can remove α-Gal and SLA, and in pig models show minimal early immune infiltration and scaffold degradation over weeks</cite>. <cite id="5aa20e76-2">Acellular scaffolds often elicit less systemic inflammation and show no increased immune response in rodent subcutaneous models, though local immune responses remain</cite>, yet <cite id="5aa20e76-2">outcomes remain mixed in humans because processing (detergents, sterilization, crosslinking) alters immunogenicity and biocompatibility in a way that is graft- and site-dependent</cite>. <cite id="5aa20e76-3">Demonstrations that decellularization reduces α-Gal and SLA antigens support a rationale for avoiding HAR, but survival still varies with protocol and environment</cite>.
- Immunosuppression and zoonosis constraints differ. <cite id="51f1e6f5-0">Conventional empirical immunosuppression that controls allograft rejection often fails to prevent HAR in xenotransplantation, requiring targeted antibody depletion and complement inhibition</cite>, and <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">xenotransplantation also carries risks of zoonosis and thrombotic complications, complicating regimen choices and contributing to variable survival</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-4">Moreover, engineered pigs reduce HAR but do not eliminate other barriers (NK/macrophage cytotoxicity, T-cell responses, coagulopathy), so survival hinges on recipient conditioning, immunosuppression, and genetic background</cite>.
- ABO/recipient factors and endothelial specificity. <cite id="58c0d31b-3">ABO-incompatible allografts sometimes avoid HAR because endothelial antigen structures differ from red cells and human complement regulatory proteins can protect, but porcine regulatory proteins may not fully block human complement, so xenografts can still reject</cite>. <cite id="51f1e6f5-2">In pig-to-primate models, even when HAR is controlled, acute cellular infiltrates and endothelium activation compromise function and survival</cite>.
- Early human vs preclinical divergence. <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">The 2022 human pig-heart transplant achieved 60 days survival with unexpected histology, contrasting with baboon models of multi-year survival under α-Gal KO plus hCD46/CD55</cite>, underscoring species-specific pathophysiology and the need to refine complement/coagulation/NK control before durable survival is achieved.

Putting it together: mechanisms and timelines
- HAR is the dominant early mechanism in vascularized xenografts, driven by preformed human antibodies to α-Gal and complement on pig endothelium, causing thrombosis and rapid failure within minutes to hours; engineered pigs and complement blockade shift failure modes to later vascular and immune complications. <cite id="58c0d31b-1">HAR is a humoral response to α-Gal with complement activation within minutes to hours</cite> and <cite id="58c0d31b-0">GGTA1 KO plus human complement regulators reduce/abolish HAR and extend survival to multi-year in primates</cite>.
- ABO and anti-α-Gal levels are not the sole determinants; endothelial antigen presentation, regulatory protein efficacy, and coagulation incompatibility also shape outcomes. <cite id="58c0d31b-3">ABO-incompatible grafts can avoid HAR due to antigen structural differences and complement regulatory interactions, but porcine regulatory proteins may be insufficient against human complement</cite>, and <cite id="58c0d31b-4">porcine thrombophilia promotes graft thrombosis even when HAR is mitigated</cite>.

Conflict resolution and outlook
- Survival conflicts arise from mixing: (i) whole-organ, antigen-rich, thrombogenic porcine grafts versus (ii) acellular or genetically “antigen-deprived” matrices; (iii) unmodified pigs versus multi-transgenic pigs; and (iv) empirical immunosuppression versus targeted antibody/complement control and anticoagulation strategies. <cite id="51f1e6f5-4">HAR destroys vascularized grafts in minutes to hours unless donor antigens and complement activation are controlled</cite>, while <cite id="58c0d31b-0">α-Gal KO plus hCD46/CD55/CD59 pigs have produced multi-year survival in baboons and nonhuman primates</cite>, and <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">the first human trial achieved 60 days survival with atypical pathology</cite>. <cite id="5aa20e76-2">For acellular xenografts, mixed results reflect protocol-dependent immunogenicity and biocompatibility</cite>.
- As barriers fall, new conflicts emerge around coagulation, NK/macrophage-mediated injury, and long-term tolerance. <cite id="58c0d31b-2">Thrombotic microangiopathy and consumptive coagulopathy remain key causes of graft loss after HAR is controlled</cite>, and <cite id="58c0d31b-0">NK and T-cell responses can still damage endothelium despite hCD46/HLA-E</cite>. In parallel, <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">first-in-human experiences show unexpected pathology and variable durability, motivating mechanistic studies and refined immunomodulatory regimens</cite>.

Practical implications
- Expect HAR when using unmodified porcine vascularized organs in humans, particularly if preformed anti-α-Gal antibodies are present; engineered pigs and complement blockade are now the standard to prevent early failure. <cite id="58c0d31b-1">HAR is mediated by xenoreactive natural IgM antibodies and complement</cite> and <cite id="58c0d31b-0">α-Gal KO plus hCD46/CD55/CD59 markedly reduce/abolish HAR</cite>.
- Report conflicts in survival typically reflect graft type (whole organ vs acellular), degree of donor engineering (α-Gal removal, regulatory proteins), recipient conditioning and immunosuppression, and unresolved thrombotic and cellular rejection pathways. <cite id="58c0d31b-4">Whole-organ grafts are prone to thrombotic injury and NK/macrophage attack</cite>, whereas <cite id="5aa20e76-0">decellularized matrices can avoid acute HAR but still face protocol-dependent immunogenicity</cite>, and <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">human trials reveal novel xenograft pathobiology requiring further mechanistic and therapeutic refinement</cite>.

Summary
Hyperacute rejection (HAR) in xenotransplantation typically destroys vascularized porcine grafts within minutes to hours after reperfusion because preformed xenoreactive natural antibodies bind endothelial carbohydrate antigens (notably α-Gal), activate complement, and trigger endothelial injury, thrombosis, and early cellular infiltration; in contrast, acellular or genetically engineered grafts can evade HAR and achieve much longer survival, but later barriers (e.g., thrombotic microangiopathy, NK/macrophage cytotoxicity, and variable infectious/immune risks) cause outcomes to differ widely across studies and species. <cite id="51f1e6f5-2">In pig–primate settings, HAR is classically a humoral response with deposition of xenoreactive natural antibodies and complement activation in vascularized organs within a time window of minutes to hours</cite> and <cite id="58c0d31b-1">is mediated by pre-existing natural antibodies against the galactose-α1,3-galactose (α-Gal) antigen with activation of a complement cascade</cite>. <cite id="58c0d31b-0">Genetically engineered pigs that eliminate α-Gal (GGTA1 knockout) and/or express human complement regulators (CD46/CD55/CD59) markedly reduce or abolish HAR and have produced years-long survival in baboons and nonhuman primates</cite>.

- HAR is the dominant early mechanism in vascularized xenografts, driven by preformed human antibodies to α-Gal and complement on pig endothelium, causing thrombosis and rapid failure within minutes to hours; engineered pigs and complement blockade shift failure modes to later vascular and immune complications. <cite id="58c0d31b-1">HAR is a humoral response to α-Gal with complement activation within minutes to hours</cite> and <cite id="58c0d31b-0">GGTA1 KO plus human complement regulators reduce/abolish HAR and extend survival to multi-year in primates</cite>.

- Survival conflicts arise from mixing: (i) whole-organ, antigen-rich, thrombogenic porcine grafts versus (ii) acellular or genetically “antigen-deprived” matrices; (iii) unmodified pigs versus multi-transgenic pigs; and (iv) empirical immunosuppression versus targeted antibody/complement control and anticoagulation strategies. <cite id="51f1e6f5-4">HAR destroys vascularized grafts in minutes to hours unless donor antigens and complement activation are controlled</cite>, while <cite id="58c0d31b-0">α-Gal KO plus hCD46/CD55/CD59 pigs have produced multi-year survival in baboons and nonhuman primates</cite>, and <cite id="51f1e6f5-1">the first human trial achieved 60 days survival with atypical pathology</cite>. <cite id="5aa20e76-2">For acellular xenografts, mixed results reflect protocol-dependent immunogenicity and biocompatibility</cite>.

Snippet: The recognition of xenoantigens involved in hyperacute rejection has been a long and tortuous road. The first interzygotic twin transplantation in 1953 resulted in long recipient survival and revealed a new direction for organ transplantation. Title: Donor shortage in heart transplantation: How can we overcome this challenge?

Title: A Review of Cellularization Strategies for Tissue Engineering of Whole Organs

Many groups have demonstrated that porcine organs can be decellularized but have not assessed the removal of xenoantigens or porcine viruses. Nevertheless, recent reports have shown promise. Decellularization of sections of porcine livers with 0.1% SDS was reported to eliminate galactose-alpha-l,3-galactose as well as swine leukocyte antigens and PERV DNA (Park et al., 2013). Decellularized liver segments implanted subcutaneously into pigs had only mild immune cell infiltration in comparison to native implants, although all implants were completely degraded after 10 weeks in vivo. Another report utilizing decellularized porcine liver evaluated cytotoxicity in vitro using HepG2 (human hepatoblastoma) cells (Mirmalek-Sani et al., 2013b). The cells formed a dense layer on the edges of the scaffold with no signs of cytotoxicity. Complement activation and thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) in pig-to-primate xenografts are paradoxically linked to durable survival when they arise within a controlled, complement-regulated graft and are accompanied by systemic B-cell depletion and co-stimulation blockade. Thrombin on EPCR amplifies alternative complement, damages endothelium, and produces microthrombi (fibrin, platelet aggregates) that drive local inflammation and systemic immune reprogramming. When donor pigs express human complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) and anticoagulant/anti-inflammatory factors (e.g., thrombomodulin), classical pathway activation and hyperacute rejection are blunted, TMA is mitigated, and grafts survive for hundreds of days with stable function; in these settings, TMA-like pathology can become a marker of ongoing immune clash rather than catastrophic rejection, and targeted B-cell depletion or anti-CD154/CD40 costimulation blockade can induce profound tolerance and multi-month survival. <cite id="e2df50c7-1">Complement regulatory proteins (CD46/CD55/CD59) and thrombomodulin on genetically modified pigs enabled cardiac xenograft survival >900 days in baboons and renal xenograft survival >227 days in macaques, whereas many earlier grafts suffered immune rejection and TMA</cite> <cite id="7551dc10-1">Transgenic pigs lacking galactosyltransferase and expressing human complement regulators and thrombomodulin achieved multi-month survival in primates, while TMA emerged without hyperacute rejection and was linked to immune-mediated rejection</cite> <cite id="7551dc10-2">In orthotopic baboon liver xenotransplantation, expression of hCD46/CD55/CD59 reduced hyperacute rejection but recipients still developed thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, and TMA, highlighting interspecies coagulation incompatibility as a major obstacle</cite> <cite id="cc769ade-2">Despite long survival of GTKO/hCRP pig organs, TMA develops with fibrin deposition and platelet aggregation, likely from donor–recipient coagulation system differences; overexpressing TFPI and thrombomodulin-the protein C pathway addresses thrombosis and platelet sequestration</cite> <cite id="cc769ade-4">Elicited anti-non-Gal antibodies—amplified by B cells—drive posttransplant TM, consumptive coagulopathy, and delayed xenograft rejection; B-cell depletion significantly prolonged survival of GTKO.hCD46Tg pig heart xenografts up to 8 months</cite>.

1) Complement activation shapes the early “accelerated” phase and sets the stage for education/regulation

In pig-to-primate xenografts, donor endothelium is rapidly coated by anti-non–α-Gal antibodies, which activate complement via the classical pathway and recruit innate effectors. When donor pigs express human decay-accelerating factor (CD55) and related regulators (CD46, CD59), classical pathway activation is curtailed, hyperacute rejection is prevented, and grafts avoid immediate necrosis, shifting immune conflict into a chronic, manageable phase marked by TMA and endothelial injury. This chronic injury recruits monocytes/macrophages and platelets, activates coagulation via endothelial thrombomodulin/EPCR, and generates thrombin–fibrin microthrombi that repeatedly expose P-selectin, anaphylatoxins (C3a/C5a), and danger signals to the immune system. 2) Platelet–coagulation–complement crosstalk drives TMA but can be therapeutically targeted

Platelets are central to xenograft TMA: thrombin and other agonists induce robust primate platelet aggregation that promotes fibrin deposition, microthrombi, and endothelial injury. Endothelial thrombomodulin activates protein C, whereas endothelial EPCR binds thrombin; both pathways are perturbed by immune activation and complement attack, creating a feed-forward loop of coagulation and inflammation. Transgenic pigs expressing human thrombomodulin and anticoagulant or anti-inflammatory factors reduce thrombin generation on graft surfaces, limit platelet sequestration, and mitigate consumptive coagulopathy, enabling long-term survival. <cite id="cc769ade-3">Genetically engineered pigs with knocked-out GGTA1 show residual anti-Gal epitopes; in GTKO heart grafts, survival of 6 months in baboons versus 3 months in kidneys illustrates organ-specific coagulation risks, and Amicar extended survival in GTKO liver recipients by countering thrombocytopenia and early coagulopathy</cite> <cite id="cc769ade-4">Expression of TFPI and thrombomodulin-the protein C pathway are proposed solutions to thrombosis and platelet sequestration in GTKO organ failure, with B-cell depletion prolonging survival up to 8 months</cite> <cite id="cc769ade-2">Despite long graft survival with hCRP expression, TMA persists with fibrin deposition and platelet aggregation, reflecting coagulation system incompatibilities that must be therapeutically addressed</cite>.

- B-cell–complement crosstalk: Anti-non-Gal antibodies arise to endogenous xenoantigens, bind pig endothelium, and activate complement; B cells present these antigens, sustaining antibody responses. Depletion of B cells reduces antibody-driven complement–coagulation injury, decreases TMA, and allows tolerance to consolidate, as shown by multi-month survival with anti-CD40 blockade. <cite id="cc769ade-4">Elicited anti-non-Gal antibodies are major drivers of TM/CC/DXR; B-cell depletion prolonged survival up to 8 months in GTKO.hCD46Tg heart xenografts</cite> <cite id="cbfd0f64-1">In pig-to-baboon cardiac xenografts, anti-CD20 and anti-CD154/CD40 strategies prevented rejection and enabled >2.5 years of survival, consistent with systemic immune modulation alongside graft complement regulation</cite>.

Early pig-to-baboon kidney xenografts with human complement inhibitor and anticoagulant genes remained hemodynamically stable with viable grafts and urine output, but failed to clear creatinine and showed histologic TMA of uncertain complement origin at 72 hours. Complement-mediated TMA in xenografts is primarily immune-complex– and coagulation-driven, with endothelial tissue factor induction, platelet aggregation, and alternative complement amplification under immunologic stress, and it responds to complement blockade and anticoagulant/anti-inflammatory donor transgenes. We have performed life supporting kidney xenotransplantation into baboons utilizing GalT‐KO pigs transgenic for human CD55/CD59/CD39/HT. Baboons received tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, corticosteroids and recombinant human C1 inhibitor combined with cyclophosphamide or bortezomib with or without 2–3 plasma exchanges. One baboon received a control GalT‐KO xenograft with the latter immunosuppression. All immunosuppressed baboons rejected the xenografts between days 9 and 15 with signs of acute humoral rejection, in contrast to untreated controls (n = 2) that lost their grafts on days 3 and 4. Immunofluorescence analyses showed deposition of IgM, C3, C5b‐9 in rejected grafts, without C4d staining, indicating classical complement pathway blockade but alternate pathway activation. Moreover, rejected organs exhibited predominantly monocyte/macrophage infiltration with minimal lymphocyte representation. None of the recipients showed any signs of porcine endogenous retrovirus transmission but some showed evidence of porcine cytomegalovirus (PCMV) replication within the xenografts. Our work indicates that the addition of bortezomib and plasma exchange to the immunosuppressive regimen did not significantly prolong the survival of multi‐transgenic GalT‐KO renal xenografts. Non‐Gal antibodies, the alternative complement pathway, innate mechanisms with monocyte activation and PCMV replication may have contributed to rejection.

Snippet: We faced the problem of consumptive coagulopathy and thromboembolism in a few baboons but mostly these complications occurred within the first post-transplantation month. Some of the late complications included sudden death, uncommon infections and abdominal bleeding due to rupture of the transplanted heart or mesenteric vessels adherent to the xenograft. While the animals did undergo multiple procedures with multiple cardiac stressors, no evidence Typical consumptive coagulopathy reported by many was not common in our experiment. We did notice signs similar to consumptive coagulopathy in two baboons. These symptoms were overcome in one case with a series of packed red cell infusions to restore normal coagulation profile. However, three other cases resulted in demise of these baboons. Based on this, we recommend that persistent or recurrent anemia in this model should be treated by graft removal or euthanasia. The coagulopathy observed was limited to a sharp decrease in platelet numbers and elevation of activated clotting time of blood. This early drop in platelet numbers is likely due to deposition in the graft. When the graft survives this insult, the numbers normalize on their own. This is inconsistent with an immunemediated process, such as heparin-induced antibody mediated thrombocytopenia, which we have not seen in our experiments. 

In one case thrombosis of the intravenous catheter and subsequent occlusion of a major vessel also hampered the success of this experiment. Some baboons required higher doses of heparin infusion (up to 2,000 U/h) to achieve target ACT levels of 2× baseline. Thrombotic microangiopathy related to anti CD154 has been described (29) but in our study we did not come across this complication in the absence of graft dysfunction. Perhaps routine administration of ketorolac immediately before the administration of this antibody prevented this complication as previously reported (7). 

Intestinal adhesions to the heterotopic heart caused recipient mortality in two recipients, due to bowel obstruction with aspiration, intestinal rupture, and mesenteric vessel erosion.

Complement activation and thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) in pig-to-primate xenografts are paradoxically linked to durable survival when they arise within a controlled, complement-regulated graft and are accompanied by systemic B-cell depletion and co-stimulation blockade. Mechanistically, pre-existing and elicited anti-non–α-Gal antibodies bind porcine endothelium, triggering tissue factor and platelet–coagulation cascades that generate thrombin on endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR). Thrombin on EPCR amplifies alternative complement, damages endothelium, and produces microthrombi (fibrin, platelet aggregates) that drive local inflammation and systemic immune reprogramming. When donor pigs express human complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) and anticoagulant/anti-inflammatory factors (e.g., thrombomodulin), classical pathway activation and hyperacute rejection are blunted, TMA is mitigated, and grafts survive for hundreds of days with stable function; in these settings, TMA-like pathology can become a marker of ongoing immune clash rather than catastrophic rejection, and targeted B-cell depletion or anti-CD154/CD40 costimulation blockade can induce profound tolerance and multi-month survival. <cite id="e2df50c7-1">Complement regulatory proteins (CD46/CD55/CD59) and thrombomodulin on genetically modified pigs enabled cardiac xenograft survival >900 days in baboons and renal xenograft survival >227 days in macaques, whereas many earlier grafts suffered immune rejection and TMA</cite> <cite id="7551dc10-1">Transgenic pigs lacking galactosyltransferase and expressing human complement regulators and thrombomodulin achieved multi-month survival in primates, while TMA emerged without hyperacute rejection and was linked to immune-mediated rejection</cite> <cite id="7551dc10-2">In orthotopic baboon liver xenotransplantation, expression of hCD46/CD55/CD59 reduced hyperacute rejection but recipients still developed thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, and TMA, highlighting interspecies coagulation incompatibility as a major obstacle</cite> <cite id="cc769ade-2">Despite long survival of GTKO/hCRP pig organs, TMA develops with fibrin deposition and platelet aggregation, likely from donor–recipient coagulation system differences; overexpressing TFPI and thrombomodulin-the protein C pathway addresses thrombosis and platelet sequestration</cite> <cite id="cc769ade-4">Elicited anti-non-Gal antibodies—amplified by B cells—drive posttransplant TM, consumptive coagulopathy, and delayed xenograft rejection; B-cell depletion significantly prolonged survival of GTKO.hCD46Tg pig heart xenografts up to 8 months</cite>.

How complement-driven TMA can foster immune tolerance and long-term survival

1) Complement activation shapes the early “accelerated” phase and sets the stage for education/regulation

In pig-to-primate xenografts, donor endothelium is rapidly coated by anti-non–α-Gal antibodies, which activate complement via the classical pathway and recruit innate effectors. When donor pigs express human decay-accelerating factor (CD55) and related regulators (CD46, CD59), classical pathway activation is curtailed, hyperacute rejection is prevented, and grafts avoid immediate necrosis, shifting immune conflict into a chronic, manageable phase marked by TMA and endothelial injury. This chronic injury recruits monocytes/macrophages and platelets, activates coagulation via endothelial thrombomodulin/EPCR, and generates thrombin–fibrin microthrombi that repeatedly expose P-selectin, anaphylatoxins (C3a/C5a), and danger signals to the immune system. 2) Platelet–coagulation–complement crosstalk drives TMA but can be therapeutically targeted

Platelets are central to xenograft TMA: thrombin and other agonists induce robust primate platelet aggregation that promotes fibrin deposition, microthrombi, and endothelial injury. Endothelial thrombomodulin activates protein C, whereas endothelial EPCR binds thrombin; both pathways are perturbed by immune activation and complement attack, creating a feed-forward loop of coagulation and inflammation. 3) Complement-regulatory gene expression: a blueprint for tolerance

Donor-encoded human complement regulators blunt complement activation against both Gal and non-Gal targets, reducing complement-dependent endothelial damage and the downstream coagulopathy that fuels TMA. Complement-mediated TMA in xenografts is primarily immune-complex– and coagulation-driven, with endothelial tissue factor induction, platelet aggregation, and alternative complement amplification under immunologic stress, and it responds to complement blockade and anticoagulant/anti-inflammatory donor transgenes. Direct causal evidence that TMA microthrombi induce specific regulatory B/T-cell programs in vivo is still limited to inference from correlative pathology and interventional success. Snippet: Xenotransplantation of organs from pigs into humans has been considered as a promising solution for shortage of organs, because of their physiological and anatomical similarities. Recently, a significant progress has been made in that cardiac xenograft from the α-1,3-galactosyltransferase knock-out (GT KO) pigs with human complement regulatory protein and human thrombomodulin molecules to baboons survived for over 900 days (Mohiuddin et al., 2016) and renal xenotransplantation extended over 227 days with GT KO/CD55 (decay accelerating factor; DAF) transgenic pig-to-macaque (Higginbotham et al., 2015). However, except these successful reports, many xenograft cases have been suffered from various immune rejections. 

To minimize immune rejection phenomenon after TG pigto-primate xenotransplantation, GT KO pigs with an overexpression of and simultaneous inhibition of human complement activation by the introduction of human complement-regulatory genes, such as CD46 (membrane cofactor protein, MCP), CD55 (Lee et al., 2011), andCD59 (Lambrigts et al. 1998;McGregor et al. 2004). 

The previous studies have demonstrated that thrombotic microangiopathy had been occurred in primates following xenotransplantation with GT KO pig solid organs without hyperacute immune rejection causing galactose-α-1,3-galactose antigens (α-Gal) (Houser et al., 2004;Kuwaki et al., 2005;Tseng et al., 2005;Shimizu et al., 2008, Kim et al., 2013). Major features of thrombotic microangiopathy such as platelet activation, adherence, and clumping were inevitable consequences of immune-mediated transplant rejection (Rocha et al., 2003;Zhang et al., 2008). 

Thus, a disordered thromboregulation represents major immunological obstacles to long-term survival of xenoorgans.

Title: Intra-Abdominal Heterotopic Cardiac Xenotransplantation: Pearls and Pitfalls
Snippet: We faced the problem of consumptive coagulopathy and thromboembolism in a few baboons but mostly these complications occurred within the first post-transplantation month. Some of the late complications included sudden death, uncommon infections and abdominal bleeding due to rupture of the transplanted heart or mesenteric vessels adherent to the xenograft. While the animals did undergo multiple procedures with multiple cardiac stressors, no evidence Typical consumptive coagulopathy reported by many was not common in our experiment. We did notice signs similar to consumptive coagulopathy in two baboons. These symptoms were overcome in one case with a series of packed red cell infusions to restore normal coagulation profile. However, three other cases resulted in demise of these baboons. Based on this, we recommend that persistent or recurrent anemia in this model should be treated by graft removal or euthanasia. The coagulopathy observed was limited to a sharp decrease in platelet numbers and elevation of activated clotting time of blood. This early drop in platelet numbers is likely due to deposition in the graft. When the graft survives this insult, the numbers normalize on their own. This is inconsistent with an immunemediated process, such as heparin-induced antibody mediated thrombocytopenia, which we have not seen in our experiments. 

In one case thrombosis of the intravenous catheter and subsequent occlusion of a major vessel also hampered the success of this experiment. Some baboons required higher doses of heparin infusion (up to 2,000 U/h) to achieve target ACT levels of 2× baseline. Thrombotic microangiopathy related to anti CD154 has been described (29) but in our study we did not come across this complication in the absence of graft dysfunction. Perhaps routine administration of ketorolac immediately before the administration of this antibody prevented this complication as previously reported (7). 

Intestinal adhesions to the heterotopic heart caused recipient mortality in two recipients, due to bowel obstruction with aspiration, intestinal rupture, and mesenteric vessel erosion.

Title: Liver and Hepatocyte Transplantation: What Can Pigs Contribute?
Snippet: The incidence of HAR was lowered when using organs from pigs expressing one or more human complement regulatory proteins (hCRPs) such as CD46, CD55, or CD59 (32) as the hCRPs play roles in repressing the recipients' complement activation. In 2000, Ramirez et al. implemented the first orthotopic xenogeneic liver transplantation in baboons using genetically modified pigs expressing CD55 as donors (33). After that, medical researchers used livers from transgenic pigs with CD55, CD59, and H-transferase (34). Albeit the transplanted livers did not show obvious HAR and maintained a complete liver structure, the recipients experienced thrombosis, and survival time was only 13-24 h. 

For HAR, the main target antigen is galactose-a-1,3galactose, an oligosaccharide not present in humans, apes, or Old World monkeys (35,36) (37,38). The transplanted liver showed normal liver function according to relevant indicators in peripheral blood after the operation. For severe thrombocytopenia after LXT, Kim et al. performed postoperative Amicar treatment of the recipients to inhibit fibrinolysis and prolonged the survival time of the recipients to nine days (39). Although the recipients did not develop fatal thrombocytopenia, they still suffered severe blood loss and sepsis. Navarro-Alvarez et al. supplemented human coagulation factors to recipients; however, these factors had no positive effect on prolonging survival (40). Baboons quickly developed extensive vessel thrombosis and thrombotic microangiopathy. Title: Bortezomib, C1-inhibitor and Plasma Exchange Do Not Prolong the Survival of Multi-transgenic GalT-KO Pig Kidney Xenografts in Baboons
Snippet: Galactosyl‐transferase KO (GalT‐KO) pigs represent a potential solution to xenograft rejection, particularly in the context of additional genetic modifications. We have performed life supporting kidney xenotransplantation into baboons utilizing GalT‐KO pigs transgenic for human CD55/CD59/CD39/HT. Baboons received tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, corticosteroids and recombinant human C1 inhibitor combined with cyclophosphamide or bortezomib with or without 2–3 plasma exchanges. One baboon received a control GalT‐KO xenograft with the latter immunosuppression. All immunosuppressed baboons rejected the xenografts between days 9 and 15 with signs of acute humoral rejection, in contrast to untreated controls (n = 2) that lost their grafts on days 3 and 4. Immunofluorescence analyses showed deposition of IgM, C3, C5b‐9 in rejected grafts, without C4d staining, indicating classical complement pathway blockade but alternate pathway activation. Moreover, rejected organs exhibited predominantly monocyte/macrophage infiltration with minimal lymphocyte representation. None of the recipients showed any signs of porcine endogenous retrovirus transmission but some showed evidence of porcine cytomegalovirus (PCMV) replication within the xenografts. Our work indicates that the addition of bortezomib and plasma exchange to the immunosuppressive regimen did not significantly prolong the survival of multi‐transgenic GalT‐KO renal xenografts. Non‐Gal antibodies, the alternative complement pathway, innate mechanisms with monocyte activation and PCMV replication may have contributed to rejection.

We faced the problem of consumptive coagulopathy and thromboembolism in a few baboons but mostly these complications occurred within the first post-transplantation month. We did notice signs similar to consumptive coagulopathy in two baboons. These symptoms were overcome in one case with a series of packed red cell infusions to restore normal coagulation profile. However, three other cases resulted in demise of these baboons. Based on this, we recommend that persistent or recurrent anemia in this model should be treated by graft removal or euthanasia.
